title: Capacity Estimation Basics
description: Learn to estimate QPS, storage, bandwidth, and memory requirements for system design interviews.

data.text: Capacity estimation converts a vague problem into concrete numbers. These numbers determine whether you need a single server or a distributed system, a relational database or a key-value store. Rough estimates are fine, but they must be reasonable and clearly stated.

terms.definition: Queries per second, a measure of request throughput.
The amount of data transferred per unit of time, often measured in gigabits per second.
The total disk space required to hold data over the system lifetime.

rows: Daily active users x Requests per user per day / 86400
Daily new data x Retention days
1 TB new per day x 365 days = 365 TB

data.caption: Step-by-step capacity estimation flow.
data.definition:
flowchart TD
    A[Start with Users] --> B[Calculate QPS]
    B --> C[Estimate Storage]
    C --> D[Calculate Bandwidth]
    D --> E[Add Growth Buffer]
    E --> F[Validate Against Single Server Limits]

data.title: Round to Powers of Ten
data.text: Use round numbers in interviews: one million users, one hundred kilobytes per request, thirty days retention. Precision is less important than reasonableness.

After you calculate your numbers, compare them against single-server limits. A modern server can handle roughly one thousand to five thousand QPS for a simple API. If your estimate exceeds that, you have justified the need for a load balancer and multiple application servers.

data.title: Estimation Checklist
points: Start with daily active users or request volume.
Add a two to three times growth buffer.
Compare against single-server limits to justify scaling.
data.takeaway: Capacity estimation turns assumptions into numbers that drive every subsequent design decision.
